lead: A digital modulator picks one of M waveforms, each lasting T seconds. Carrying M functions is clumsy. Instead each waveform is drawn as a point. Two signals are compared by an inner product, an integral over one symbol. The M points live in at most M dimensions, and Gram-Schmidt builds the axes. Energy becomes squared length, distance becomes separation, and the matched filter and error probability (see 5.5 and 5.6) are geometry on that picture.
prereq: You need orthogonality of sinusoids and the Fourier transform from Unit 1, Foundations: Signals, Noise and Random Processes.

blocks.text: Two real signals lasting 0 ≤ t < T are compared by an inner product: multiply and integrate.

blocks.where: ⟨x,y⟩ is the inner product; T is symbol duration in seconds; x,y in volts give V²·s (or V²·ms).

blocks.text: The norm is length; its square is energy.

blocks.where: ‖x‖ is norm in V·√s; E_x = ∫₀ᵀ x²(t) dt is energy in V²·s, the energy a 1 Ω resistor would absorb.

blocks.text: An orthonormal basis has unit-norm, mutually orthogonal axes φᵢ.
⟨φᵢ, φⱼ⟩ = 1 if i = j, and 0 if i ≠ j
blocks.where: φᵢ,φⱼ are axes; each φᵢ carries 1/√s when signals are in volts, so its energy is the pure number 1.

blocks.text: With N axes, a signal is a weighted sum; each weight is an inner product.
s_m(t) = Σᵢ₌₁ᴺ s_mi φᵢ(t),  s_mi = ⟨s_m, φᵢ⟩
blocks.where: s_m(t) is the mth signal; s_mi is its ith coordinate in V·√s; N is the number of axes.

blocks.text: Energy is the sum of squared coordinates. Squared distance is the sum of squared coordinate differences.
E_m = Σᵢ s_mi²,   d²(m, n) = Σᵢ (s_mi − s_ni)²
blocks.where: E_m is energy in V²·s; d(m,n) is distance in V·√s; s_mi,s_ni are coordinates. Distance is not E_m − E_n.

blocks.text: Gram-Schmidt takes signals one at a time and removes the part already explained by existing axes.

items: Next signal s_m: cᵢ = ⟨s_m, φᵢ⟩ on every existing axis.
Residual: g_m = s_m − Σᵢ cᵢ φᵢ.
If ‖g_m‖ = 0, s_m is already explained; skip it.
If ‖g_m‖ ≠ 0, add φ_new = g_m/‖g_m‖ and increase N.
Repeat for m = 2, 3, …, M. The final dimension count obeys N ≤ M.

blocks.text: Check orthogonality: ⟨g_m, φ_k⟩ = ⟨s_m, φ_k⟩ − Σᵢ cᵢ⟨φᵢ, φ_k⟩ = c_k − c_k = 0. All φ_k content was subtracted; nothing across it changed.
Signal order changes which axes appear, not energies or distances between points.
No inner product exceeds the product of the norms. This is Cauchy-Schwarz.

blocks.where: |⟨x,y⟩| is absolute inner product; ‖x‖,‖y‖ are norms. Equality holds only when y = c x for a constant c.

blocks.text: For received r, the filter sample is ⟨r, s⟩ = ⟨s, s⟩ + ⟨n, s⟩. For a fixed received energy and a fixed reference energy ‖s‖², ⟨r, s⟩ is largest when s has exactly the incoming shape; the largest value is ‖r‖‖s‖. No filter beats it; see 5.5.
PAM uses one shape p(t): φ₁ = p/‖p‖, and level A_m becomes the scalar A_m‖p‖. BPSK has two points on one line, +√E and −√E, separated by 2√E.

QPSK needs cosine and sine axes at the same carrier frequency. Its four points lie on a circle of radius √E at π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4. Neighbours are √(2E) apart; opposites are 2√E apart. Passband constellations belong to Unit 6.

figure.caption: Each signal is projected on the axes found so far, the projection is subtracted, and a non-zero leftover is normalised into a new axis; a zero leftover is skipped.

spec.title: Gram-Schmidt in one pass
spec.aria: Each signal is projected on the axes already found, the projection is subtracted, and a non-zero leftover is normalised into a new axis, while a zero leftover is skipped and the next signal is taken.

examples.question: Over 0 ≤ t < T with T = 1 ms, s₁(t) = 1 V for the whole interval and s₂(t) = 2 V for the first half and 0 V for the second half. Work in units of V·√ms. (a) Find φ₁ and φ₂ by Gram-Schmidt. (b) Give the coordinates of s₁ and s₂. (c) Find both energies and the distance between the points. (d) Check Cauchy-Schwarz for the pair.
steps: E₁ = ∫₀¹ (1)² dt = 1 V²·ms, so ‖s₁‖ = 1 V·√ms and φ₁ = s₁/‖s₁‖ = 1 V / (1 V·√ms) = 1/√ms over the whole interval — unit energy.
⟨s₂, φ₁⟩ = ∫₀¹ s₂(t)·(1/√ms) dt = 2×0.5 + 0×0.5 = 1 V·√ms. Each half is 0.5 ms.
g₂ = s₂ − 1·φ₁ = +1 V over the first half and −1 V over the second half.
‖g₂‖² = 1²×0.5 + (−1)²×0.5 = 1 V²·ms, so ‖g₂‖ = 1 V·√ms. Non-zero: φ₂ = g₂/‖g₂‖ = +1/√ms over the first half and −1/√ms over the second.
Energies from coordinates: E₁ = 1² + 0² = 1 V²·ms; E₂ = 1² + 1² = 2 V²·ms. Waveform check: ∫₀¹ s₂² dt = 4×0.5 = 2 V²·ms.
Cauchy-Schwarz: |⟨s₁, s₂⟩| = 1 V²·ms while ‖s₁‖‖s₂‖ = 1×√2 = 1.414 V²·ms. Since 1 ≤ 1.414 the bound holds; it is not tight because s₂ is not a multiple of s₁.
examples.answer: φ₁ = 1/√ms over the whole interval, φ₂ = ±1/√ms over the two halves; s₁ = (1, 0) and s₂ = (1, 1) V·√ms; energies 1 and 2 V²·ms; distance 1 V·√ms; Cauchy-Schwarz gives 1 ≤ 1.414 V²·ms.
examples.check:
import math

h = 0.5                  # each half is 0.5 ms; T = 1 ms
s1 = [1.0, 1.0]          # volts, first half then second half
s2 = [2.0, 0.0]

E1 = sum(v * v * h for v in s1)
n1 = math.sqrt(E1)
print(E1)
print(n1)

phi1 = [v / n1 for v in s1]
c21 = sum(a * p * h for a, p in zip(s2, phi1))
print(c21)

g2 = [b - c21 * a for a, b in zip(phi1, s2)]
n2 = math.sqrt(sum(v * v * h for v in g2))
print(n2)

phi2 = [v / n2 for v in g2]
c11 = sum(a * p * h for a, p in zip(s1, phi1))
c12 = sum(a * p * h for a, p in zip(s1, phi2))
c21 = sum(a * p * h for a, p in zip(s2, phi1))
c22 = sum(a * p * h for a, p in zip(s2, phi2))
print(c21 ** 2 + c22 ** 2)
print(math.sqrt((c11 - c21) ** 2 + (c12 - c22) ** 2))
print(n1 * math.sqrt(c21 ** 2 + c22 ** 2))

traps: Using N = M in the error formula. Dependent signals are skipped, so N can be smaller than the number of signals; N ≤ M, not equal to M.
Confusing energy and squared distance. Energy is Σ s_mi² from the origin; squared distance is Σ (s_mi − s_ni)². It is never E_m − E_n.
Forgetting normalisation. Using g_m as an axis instead of g_m/‖g_m‖ makes every later coordinate, energy and distance wrong.
Dropping units. Inner products carry V²·s, norms and coordinates carry V·√s, and axes carry 1/√s. Unitless answers lose marks.
Believing the basis is unique. A different signal order gives different axes and hence different coordinates; only the energies and the distances between points stay the same.

quiz.q: Define the inner product and the norm of two real signals over 0 ≤ t < T, and give the unit of each.
quiz.a: ⟨x, y⟩ = ∫₀ᵀ x(t)y(t) dt in V²·s; ‖x‖ = √⟨x, x⟩ = √E_x in V·√s, where E_x is signal energy.

quiz.q: State the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the condition for equality.
quiz.a: |⟨x, y⟩| ≤ ‖x‖‖y‖. Equality only when y = c x: one signal is a scaled copy of the other.

quiz.q: Why can the number of dimensions N be smaller than the number of signals M?
quiz.a: A signal that is a linear combination of existing axes has zero residual and adds no direction. Three signals with s₃ = s₁ + s₂ still need only two axes.

quiz.q: T = 2 ms. s₁(t) = 1 V for the whole interval. s₂(t) = +1 V for the first 1 ms and −1 V for the second 1 ms. Find φ₁, φ₂, the coordinates and the distance between the points.
quiz.a: E₁ = 1²×2 = 2 V²·ms, so ‖s₁‖ = √2 V·√ms and φ₁ = s₁/√2. ⟨s₂, φ₁⟩ = 1/√2 − 1/√2 = 0, so g₂ = s₂, ‖g₂‖ = √2 and φ₂ = s₂/√2. Coordinates: s₁ = (√2, 0), s₂ = (0, √2) V·√ms. d = √(2 + 2) = 2 V·√ms.

quiz.q: In the worked example s₂ has coordinates (1, 1) V·√ms. Compute its energy from the coordinates and confirm it from the waveform.
quiz.a: Energy = 1² + 1² = 2 V²·ms. From the waveform, ∫₀¹ s₂² dt = 4×0.5 + 0×0.5 = 2 V²·ms. They agree.

quiz.q: Show that after Gram-Schmidt the residual g_m is orthogonal to every axis already found.
quiz.a: ⟨g_m, φ_k⟩ = ⟨s_m, φ_k⟩ − Σᵢ cᵢ⟨φᵢ, φ_k⟩ with cᵢ = ⟨s_m, φᵢ⟩. Orthonormality kills every term except i = k, leaving c_k − c_k = 0. So g_m is perpendicular to all old axes.

quiz.q: All M signals in a set have the same energy E. Bound |⟨s_m, s_n⟩| and say when the bound is tight.
quiz.a: By Cauchy-Schwarz, |⟨s_m, s_n⟩| ≤ ‖s_m‖‖s_n‖ = √E·√E = E. Equality needs s_n = c s_m; equal energies force c = ±1. Identical signals (c = +1) reach |⟨s_m, s_n⟩| = E with zero distance between the points — the worst case for a detector. Antipodal signals (c = −1) also reach the bound, but at the maximum distance 2√E — the best case.

beyond: Not for the exam. Signal space underlies coding and modulation design: packing M points in N dimensions is sphere packing. MIMO adds space as axes, so space-time codes are signal sets of matrices. Noncoherent systems use Grassmannian spaces. In software, stable Gram-Schmidt is QR decomposition (numpy.linalg.qr, scipy.linalg.orth). Searches: QR decomposition, sphere packing constellation, MIMO signal space, Grassmannian constellation.
